---
title: "Return and continue your work"
---

You have ended your previous JupyterLab session.

Now you will start a **new** computing environment and confirm what was preserved.

This is the final part of the persistence test.

## 1. Start a new JupyterLab environment

Return to DNAnexus and start a new JupyterLab environment using the same project as before.

Use the same settings from **Start JupyterLab**:

- **Snapshot:** leave blank;
- **Cluster Configuration:** Single Node;
- **Instance Type:** `mem1_ssd1_v2_x4`; and
- **Feature:** `PYTHON_R`.

Wait until the environment shows **Ready**, then select **Open**.

::: {.callout-note title="This is a new temporary computer"}
The JupyterLab environment you used previously has ended.

The environment you are starting now is a **new temporary computing environment** connected to the same persistent DNAnexus project.
:::

## 2. Reopen your `[DX]` notebook

Use the **DNAnexus project browser** to return to your workspace.

Open:

```text
getting-started.ipynb
```

Check that the notebook tab again shows:

```text
[DX] getting-started.ipynb
```

## 3. Check what survived

Before running any code, scroll through the notebook.

You should still be able to see:

- the R code you ran;
- the first rows of the synthetic dataset;
- the output from `dim()` and `summary()`;
- the summary table; and
- the figure.

These were saved as part of your persistent `[DX]` notebook.

::: {.callout-success title="Your notebook persisted"}
The previous JupyterLab computing environment has ended, but your saved notebook and its displayed outputs remain in the DNAnexus project.

This is why `[DX]` notebooks are useful for keeping a persistent record of an analysis.
:::

## 4. Check the new R session

Now we will test whether the R object `dat` also survived.

**Do not rerun any of the earlier notebook cells yet.**

Find the section:

**7. After restarting JupyterLab**

Run:

```r
exists("dat")
```

You should see:

```text
[1] FALSE
```

This means that `dat` does not exist in the new R session.

Nothing has gone wrong.

The previous `dat` object existed only in the memory of the R session that ended with your previous JupyterLab environment.

## 5. Recreate `dat`

Return to the earlier section:

**2. Read the training data**

Rerun:

```r
dat <- read.csv(
  "/mnt/project/mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/data/example_data.csv"
)

head(dat)
```

You have now recreated `dat` from the persistent CSV file stored in the DNAnexus project.

To confirm this, run:

```r
exists("dat")
```

again.

This time you should see:

```text
[1] TRUE
```

::: {.callout-tip title="This is reproducibility in action"}
You did not need the old R session to continue your work.

The project still contained the original data, and your notebook still contained the code needed to recreate the R object.

Running the code again restored the object you needed.
:::

## 6. The key idea

You have now directly tested the difference between persistent storage and temporary computing.

| Item | After ending and restarting JupyterLab |
|---|---|
| DNAnexus project | **Still there** |
| `example_data.csv` | **Still there** |
| Saved `[DX]` notebook | **Still there** |
| Saved code | **Still there** |
| Saved displayed tables and figures | **Still there** |
| Previous JupyterLab environment | **Ended** |
| Previous R session | **Ended** |
| `dat` in R memory | **Gone until recreated** |

The workflow can be summarized as:

<div class="mcps-workflow-summary">

**Persistent project + saved code → new JupyterLab session → rerun code → continue analysis**

</div>

## 7. Continue rather than start again

In real analyses, you will often work across several JupyterLab sessions.

You do not need to rebuild your analysis manually each time.

Instead:

1. keep your code in a persistent `[DX]` notebook;
2. save the notebook regularly;
3. end JupyterLab when you finish working;
4. start a new environment when you return;
5. reopen the same `[DX]` notebook; and
6. rerun the code needed to recreate your R objects.

::: {.callout-note title="Your notebook is the recipe"}
A useful way to think about this is:

**The project stores the ingredients.**

**The notebook stores the recipe.**

**The temporary R session is where you prepare the analysis.**

When you return later, you can use the same ingredients and recipe to recreate what you need.
:::

## 8. Save and end this test session

You have completed the persistence exercise.

Save `getting-started.ipynb` once more.

If you do not need the JupyterLab environment for anything else, end it using:

**DNAnexus → End Session**

## Checkpoint

You should now be able to explain the following distinction:

> **Files and saved `[DX]` notebooks in the DNAnexus project are persistent. JupyterLab environments and live R objects are temporary.**

::: {.callout-success title="Persistence test complete"}
You have successfully ended a JupyterLab session, returned in a new environment, reopened your saved analysis, and recreated a temporary R object from persistent project data.

You now understand the core DNAnexus workflow used throughout the MCPS training materials.
:::
